title: The for Loop
description: Repeat a block a known number of times with a counter you control.

content.value: Every program so far ran each line once. Computers shine when they do the same job again and again, without getting bored or making a typo.

content.real: Writing a line 300 times by hand
content.text: By hand, 300 lines takes an afternoon. A **loop** is code that repeats. You write the action once, and the loop counts the turns for you.

content.caption: Both halves print the same lines. Changing `3` to `300` in the loop is a one-character edit. The long way would need 297 more lines.

parts.label: start
parts.note: Runs once, before the first turn. Makes the counter `i`.

parts.label: condition
parts.note: Tested before every turn. True: run the body. False: stop.

parts.label: update
parts.note: Runs after every turn. Adds 1 to `i`.

content.title: Anatomy of a for loop
content.caption: Semicolons split the three parts. The counter is usually called `i`, short for index. When it means something real, name it: `row`, `day`, `attempt`.

steps.note: Start: `int i = 0` runs once. Then the condition `0 < 3` is true, so the body runs.
`i++` makes `i` 3. Check `3 < 3`: false, so the loop ends.
The program carries on below the loop. `i` belonged to the loop, so it no longer exists.

content.title: Watch the loop go round
content.outro: Start once, then check, body, update, check, body, update... until the check is false.

content.question: How many lines does this print?
content.explain: `i` takes the values 0, 1, 2 and 3. When it reaches 4, `4 < 4` is false and the loop stops. Four turns, four lines.

content.value: The condition is tested **before** every turn, even the first. If `items` is 0, then `for (int i = 1; i <= items; i++)` runs zero times. That is often exactly what you want.
content.title: A loop can run zero times

content.value: Change the start, the condition or the update and you get any sequence you like: downwards with `i--`, or in steps of 2 with `i += 2`.

endl inside
items.text: Each number on its own line.

content.title: One line or many?
content.caption: To build one line out of many turns, print the pieces with no `endl`, then end the line once with `cout << endl;` after the loop.
`7 * i` needs no brackets: C++ works out the maths before `<<` prints it. Do not glue a number onto text with `+`: `"Line " + i` compiles but prints something strange. Use `<<` for each piece.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: Start at 10 and take away 3 each turn: 10, 7, 4, 1. The next value, -2, fails `i > 0`, so it never prints.

content.value: A loop can build up an answer. Declare a variable **before** the loop, then change it on every turn. A running total like this is called an **accumulator**.

steps.note: The total starts at 0, so adding to it does not change the answer.
`i` becomes 5. `5 <= 4` is false: the loop ends.
`total` was declared outside the loop, so it still exists here.

content.title: Watch the total grow

items.sub: Adding 0 does not change the answer.
Multiplying by 1 does not change the answer: `product *= i`.
Then it still exists when the loop has finished.

content.caption: Sample run: type 2, then 7 and 8. It prints `Total: 15` and `Average: 7.5`. The same lines handle 3 numbers or 3000. `static_cast<double>` stops whole-number division turning 7.5 into 7.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: `product` starts at 1, then becomes 1, 2, 6 and 24. That is 1 x 2 x 3 x 4.

content.value: Most loop bugs are **off-by-one**: the loop runs one time too many or one too few. It usually comes down to `<` against `<=`.

items.title: i <= 5
i < 5

content.title: <= vs <
content.caption: `for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++)` also runs five times, it just counts 0 to 4. When a loop gives one result too few, look here first.

output: This prints once, not three times.
content.caption: A `;` right after the brackets gives the loop an empty body, the same trap you met with `if`. The loop spins doing nothing, then the block below runs once.

content.value: `i` belongs to the loop. After the closing brace, using it is a compile error: `'i' was not declared in this scope`. To keep the counter, declare `int i;` above the loop and write `for (i = 1; i <= 5; i++)`.

quiz.question: What are the three parts inside `for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++)`, in order?
options: The start value, the update, and the condition
The start value, the condition to keep going, and the update after each turn
The condition, the start value, and the end value
quiz.explain: Start, condition, update. C++ runs the start once, then tests the condition before every turn and runs the update after every turn.

quiz.question: How many times does the block in `for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++)` run?
quiz.explain: It runs with i as 0, 1, 2 and 3, which is four turns. Starting at 0 with `<` is the same count as starting at 1 with `<=`.

quiz.question: Why must an accumulator like `int total = 0;` be declared before the loop?
options: So it survives the loop, instead of being created fresh on every turn
Because C++ does not allow new variables inside a loop
quiz.explain: A variable declared inside the block is created and destroyed on every turn, so it could never build up a total, and it would not exist after the loop either.

quiz.question: What does `for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++);` followed by a block print, if that block has one `cout` in it?
options: The line once, because the semicolon gave the loop an empty body
quiz.explain: The semicolon ends the loop immediately, so it repeats nothing. The block below is then an ordinary block and runs once.

quiz.question: Where does `i` exist in a `for (int i = ...)` loop?
options: Only inside the loop: using it afterwards is a compile error
quiz.explain: Declaring the counter in the brackets keeps it local to the loop. Declare it on the line above if you need its final value later.
